articles.title: Anatomical Study of the Biceps Sheath for Safe and Accurate Unguided Anterior Shoulder Injections.
articles.authors: Shimizu Keigo, Yoko Tabira, Tatsuya Harano et al.
articles.abstract: The tendon of the long head of the biceps brachii (LHBT) contributes to shoulder joint stability, but can become a source of shoulder pain because of trauma or degeneration. Injection of local anesthetics into the biceps sheath (BS) is an effective treatment for managing anterior shoulder pain and is widely performed clinically; however, the accuracy of unguided injections remains low. This study aimed to clarify the anatomical characteristics of the BS and identify the optimal injection site to improve the accuracy and safety of unguided anterior shoulder injections. Eight 5% formalin-fixed cadavers (16 shoulders) and 1 Thiel-embalmed cadaver were examined at Kurume University School of Medicine. Morphological measurements and histological evaluations were performed on cadaveric shoulders. In addition, ultrasound examinations were performed on 28 shoulders from 14 healthy adults. Vascular distribution around the BS was evaluated using latex injection in the Thiel-embalmed cadaver. The mean BS length in cadavers was 36.2 ± 8.4 mm, and the mean width was 9.4 ± 1.2 mm; these were not significantly different than those in live subjects. Macroscopic observations confirmed continuity between the BS and the shoulder joint capsule. The anterior circumflex humeral artery ran along the lateral aspect of the LHBT, while the transverse humeral ligament was located approximately 23 mm proximal to the BS. The BS is continuous with the joint capsule, and injections into the BS allow intra-articular delivery of medication. The optimal injection site is approximately 1.5 transverse fingerbreadths distal to the superomedial edge of the greater tubercle and medial to the LHBT. This location minimizes the risk of injuring the anterior circumflex humeral artery and the extended tendon of the subscapularis muscle while improving the accuracy of needle placement.

articles.title: A Novel Patient-Specific Landmark-Guided Approach for Intramuscular Botulinum Neurotoxin Injections Into the Rotator Cuff: A Cadaveric Study.
articles.authors: Dave Osinachukwu Duru, David Kwan Ryung Lee, Gavin E Jarvis et al.
articles.abstract: Myofascial pain syndrome (MFPS) causes chronic shoulder pain. Supraspinatus and infraspinatus, rotator cuff muscles innervated by the suprascapular nerve, are commonly affected. Intramuscular botulinum neurotoxin (BoNT) injections near motor points (i.e., visible nerve branch entry sites used as a proxy for motor endplates) are an effective treatment for such pain. However, current techniques limit accessibility. This study aimed to develop a patient-specific, landmark-guided technique for BoNT delivery into supraspinatus and infraspinatus using scapular dimensions. Ten pairs of cadaveric shoulders (n = 20) were dissected to identify supraspinatus and infraspinatus motor points. Distances from scapular landmarks to these motor points were measured in two axes. These distances were correlated with scapular dimensions (height, spine length, width) using linear regression. Patient-specific predictive formulae were derived. For validation, landmark-guided methylene blue dye injections were performed on four additional shoulders using calculated coordinates. For supraspinatus, motor points were predicted using deltoid tubercle and root of the scapular spine (r = 0.58-0.64, p = 0.0016-0.021). For infraspinatus, root of the scapular spine and lateral acromion were used (r = 0.46-0.60, p = 0.0054-0.0500). In all validation specimens, injected dye accurately reached the motor points. This study provides a validated, patient-specific, landmark-guided technique for BoNT delivery into the rotator cuff, offering an approach for accessible analgesia.

articles.title: A new species of Lonchidiidae (Hybodontiformes) from the Late Jurassic of Brazil (Aliança Formation, Jatobá Basin).
articles.authors: Larissa de Souza Ribeiro, Marco Aurélio Gallo de França
articles.abstract: The Aliança Formation (Jatobá Basin) represents lacustrine deposits formed in oxygenated waters that hosted a diverse fauna, including Hybodontiform sharks. Within this group, the Family Lonchidiidae comprises 11 valid genera, with Parvodus previously reported in Brazilian deposits from the Brejo Santo Formation (Araripe Basin, Late Jurassic) and the Aliança Formation (Jatobá Basin, Late Jurassic). Here, we describe a new species of Parvodus based on isolated teeth from the Aliança Formation. A taxonomic reassessment of the genus is also presented, integrating its stratigraphic and geographic distribution. The new species provides novel insights into the evolutionary history of Lonchidiidae, with implications for the paleobiogeography of the group and the paleoenvironmental interpretation of the Aliança Formation. Importantly, this record expands the known distribution of Parvodus into the Upper Jurassic of South America.

articles.title: Medical students' perceptions of smartphone-derived three-dimensional cadaveric models for anatomy education: a cross-sectional study.
articles.authors: Eren Ogut, Esma Büşra Yildirim, Sude Naz Kilic et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Smartphone-based photogrammetry may provide an accessible way to create reusable three-dimensional (3D) models from cadaveric specimens for anatomy education. This study evaluated medical students' perceptions of these models and explored factors associated with their overall evaluations. METHODS: This cross-sectional study included 100 medical students who evaluated images and linked videos of smartphone-derived cadaveric models using a 22-item Likert-type questionnaire. Group differences were examined using non-parametric tests. Internal consistency, preliminary factor analysis, Spearman correlations, and exploratory multiple linear regression were also assessed. RESULTS: Participating students generally evaluated the model materials positively. The highest-rated items concerned long-term reuse through a digital model library (4.28 ± 0.59), improved access when cadaveric material is limited (4.26 ± 0.71), support for 3D thinking in interventional or surgical settings (4.22 ± 0.60), and preparation for clinical clerkships (4.19 ± 0.53). Regular integration into anatomy teaching was supported by 82% of participants. No significant differences were observed by sex or year of study. After reverse scoring negatively worded items, Cronbach's alpha was 0.881. Age group showed a weak correlation with the exploratory overall evaluation score (r = 0.286, p = 0.004). The exploratory regression model explained 11.4% of the variance but was not statistically significant (R2 = 0.114, p = 0.122). CONCLUSION: Participating medical students generally viewed smartphone-derived cadaveric digital models favorably, particularly for repeated access and the development of digital specimen libraries. These findings describe perceived usefulness and acceptability; they do not establish improvements in anatomical knowledge, spatial ability, or retention. Controlled studies using objective learning outcomes are needed before educational effectiveness can be determined.

articles.title: The tibialis posterior tendon revisited: a classification-based anatomical and radiological framework.
articles.authors: Łukasz Olewnik, Ingrid C Landfald, Piotr Łabętowicz et al.
articles.abstract: The tibialis posterior tendon (TPT) demonstrates substantial anatomical variability in its branching and attachment morphology, extending beyond the simplified concept of a predominantly navicular attachment. This narrative review critically reappraises the classification of TPT attachment patterns proposed by Olewnik and places it in the context of subsequent anatomical, radiological, and functional evidence. Later anatomical studies have confirmed extensive variation in the number, distribution, and surface area of TPT attachments and have identified configurations not represented within the original classification. These findings support the use of classification systems as structured descriptive frameworks rather than exhaustive catalogues of TPT morphology. Cadaveric imaging studies demonstrate that complex TPT branching and attachment anatomy can be depicted on MRI; however, individual anatomical types and subtypes have not undergone systematic radiological validation. Representative MRI examples are therefore included for anatomical illustration rather than as diagnostic criteria. The functional significance of individual attachment patterns and their potential relationship to hindfoot and midfoot joint morphology remain incompletely understood. Further anatomical, imaging, and biomechanical studies are required to determine whether specific TPT patterns have reproducible radiological or functional correlates.

articles.title: CFD simulations of the gait cycle in running aerodynamics from a quasi-static perspective.
articles.authors: Xiaoqi Hu, Fabio Malizia, Costin Ioan Coșoiu et al.
articles.abstract: Running is a highly dynamic locomotion process, yet most existing aerodynamic studies approximate the runner using a single static posture. This study presents a validated computational fluid dynamics investigation of posture-dependent running aerodynamics throughout the gait cycle from a quasi-static perspective. Five representative gait-cycle postures are analysed for a male runner. The results reveal substantial aerodynamic variations throughout the gait cycle with maximum drag occurring for the mid-stance and minimum drag for the flight postures. Relative to the minimum-drag posture, the peak drag area increases by approximately 20.6%. Flow-field analysis shows that changes in leg configuration strongly influence wake development. The toe-off and flight postures are characterised by a partially interrupted torso wake and more compact wake structures, whereas the higher-drag postures exhibit broader low-velocity wake regions. Body-part decomposition further indicates that the torso is the dominant drag contributor, accounting for approximately 50-59% of the total drag area, while the upper legs exhibit the strongest posture sensitivity. The findings provide new physical insights into posture-dependent running aerodynamics and establish a foundation for future investigations of fully dynamic running motion.

articles.title: Methodological considerations in estimating active muscle stiffness index.
articles.authors: Ophélie Larivière, Manon Dauvergne, Florian Etheve et al.
articles.abstract: Accurate quantification of muscle stiffness using shear wave elastography is essential for evaluating neuromuscular function. The active muscle stiffness index, derived from the relationship between shear modulus and force, can be estimated using either continuous ramp or discrete step approaches, which are often considered equivalent. This study aimed to directly compare these two approaches. Thirty healthy women performed isometric knee extensions up to 50% of maximal voluntary contraction under both ramp and step contractions, while shear wave elastography measurements were obtained from the vastus lateralis. The active muscle stiffness index was calculated for each protocol. Agreement between methods was evaluated using paired t-tests, Lin's concordance correlation coefficient, and Bland-Altman analysis. Results revealed a significant difference between protocols (p < 0.001). Although a very strong correlation was observed (r ≈ 0.88), concordance was lower (CCC ≈ 0.81). Bland-Altman analysis indicated a systematic bias of -0.20 kPa/Nm (∼20%) without proportional bias. These findings demonstrate that ramp and step approaches yield systematically different estimates and should not be considered interchangeable.

articles.title: Whole-body angular momentum regulation during Tai Chi stepping: Task- and experience-related differences.
articles.authors: Leichao Liang, Yuzhao Xie, He Li et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Tai Chi stepping involves slow progression, prolonged weight transfer, and coordinated trunk-limb rotation, but its whole-body angular momentum regulation remains poorly understood. RESEARCH QUESTION: How do whole-body angular momentum regulation patterns differ across the tested movement conditions of normal gait (NG), Brush Knee Twist Step (BKT), and Repulse Monkey (RM) at self-selected speeds, and between experienced and novice-level practitioners? METHODS: Seventeen experienced and 14 novice-level Tai Chi practitioners performed NG, BKT, and RM. In each anatomical plane, whole-body angular momentum excursion and intersegmental cancellation were quantified over the movement cycle, and bilateral external-moment cancellation during the double-support phases. Outcomes were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models. RESULTS: BKT and RM were slower than NG (0.14-0.23 vs. 1.28-1.29 m/s) and had longer total double-support duration (approximately 69% vs. 23% of the cycle). Relative to NG, both showed greater transverse-plane angular momentum excursion (6.5-10.4 × 10-3 vs. 1.9-2.2 × 10-3), higher frontal-plane intersegmental cancellation (46-55% vs. 39-41%) but lower sagittal- and transverse-plane intersegmental cancellation (19-38% vs. 76-82%), and higher sagittal-plane bilateral external-moment cancellation (87-90% vs. 29%). During RM, experienced practitioners had smaller angular momentum excursion in all planes and higher transverse-plane bilateral external-moment cancellation (50.1% vs. 30.5%); a wider step width was also observed in the experienced group (0.109 vs. 0.061 m). SIGNIFICANCE: Relative to NG, Tai Chi stepping showed movement- and plane-specific patterns of angular momentum regulation, with experience-related differences clearest during RM. These findings indicate that whole-body angular momentum regulation can be quantified as a biomechanical feature of Tai Chi stepping tasks.

articles.title: Biomechanical effects of a semi-rigid knee orthotic during walking in individuals with medial knee osteoarthritis.
articles.authors: Pauline Göbel, Batın Yılmazgün, Stefan Sell et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Medial knee osteoarthritis is associated with increased medial compartment loading during gait. Valgus unloader knee orthotics are commonly used to reduce medial knee loading, but the biomechanical responses associated with semi-rigid designs remain unclear. RESEARCH QUESTION: After six weeks of use, what effect does the orthotic condition have on first-peak knee adduction moment (KAM), second-peak KAM, and knee adduction angular impulse (KAAI) during constant-speed and self-selected-speed walking compared with baseline in individuals with medial knee osteoarthritis? METHODS: Twenty-four participants with Kellgren-Lawrence grade 2-4 completed a within-participant pretest-posttest study. Gait was assessed without the orthotic at baseline and while wearing it after six weeks of use (mean 5.13 h/day), at a constant speed of 1.39 m/s and self-selected speed. In OpenSim, first-peak KAM, second-peak KAM, and KAAI were calculated. GRF variables were secondary, exploratory outcomes. Conditions were compared using paired t-tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Holm-Bonferroni adjustment was applied to the three KAM-related outcomes within each walking condition. RESULTS: During constant-speed walking, first-peak KAM, second-peak KAM, and KAAI were lower with the orthotic by 6.9% , (r = 0.44), 6.8% (r = 0.47), and 15.8% (r = 0.51), respectively (Holm-adjusted p = 0.045 for each). Vertical GRF variables did not differ, whereas the braking-peak magnitude and braking and propulsive impulses increased. During self-selected-speed, participants walked 15.5% faster in the orthotic condition (p < 0.001). First- and second-peak KAM did not differ significantly from baseline, whereas KAAI was lower (-0.030 N·m·kg⁻¹·s, 95% CI -0.050 to -0.010; Holm-adjusted p = 0.014). The first vertical, braking, and propulsive GRF peaks increased, while vertical impulse decreased. SIGNIFICANCE: Semi-rigid orthotic use was associated with lower KAM-related loading during constant-speed walking and faster self-selected walking without higher peak KAM. The semi-rigid orthotic may be considered a possible adjunct to individualized, multicomponent care for individuals with medial knee osteoarthritis.

articles.title: Postural adjustments in standing and gait reflect amnestic mild cognitive impairment.
articles.authors: Yi-Chun Kuan, Shiuan-Huei Lu, Cheng-Hao Yu et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Amnestic mild cognitive impairment (aMCI), a prodromal stage of Alzheimer's disease, may involve subtle motor alterations preceding overt cognitive decline. Because postural alignment integrates multisensory and executive control systems, it may reveal early motor-cognitive disruption. This study aimed to identify posture-related features associated with cognition and to determine whether individuals with aMCI exhibit distinct standing and gait kinematics. METHODS: In this cross-sectional observational study, 14 older adults with aMCI and 14 age-matched cognitively healthy controls underwent three-dimensional motion analysis during quiet standing and level walking. Segmental angles and temporospatial gait parameters were analysed. Cognitive performance was assessed using standardised neuropsychological tests. Group comparisons and exploratory partial correlation analyses adjusted for age and education were performed. RESULTS: The aMCI group exhibited reduced lumbar extension (p = 0.020), pelvic anterior tilt (p = 0.012), and hip flexion (p = 0.016) during standing. While lumbopelvic deviations persisted during gait (p ≤ 0.011), hip flexion and temporospatial parameters were comparable between groups. In controls, verbal episodic memory correlated positively with lumbopelvic alignment (r = 0.67-0.80, p ≤ 0.02). In aMCI, greater hip flexion during gait was associated with poor verbal fluency (r = -0.57, p = 0.05) and visual memory (r = -0.68, p = 0.02). CONCLUSIONS: Lumbopelvic alignment was closely linked to episodic memory in cognitively normal ageing, but this coupling appeared disrupted in aMCI, with motor-cognitive associations shifting toward hip-mediated compensatory or reorganised gait control. These kinematic markers were detectable despite preserved gait speed and may be more sensitive than conventional temporospatial gait measures under steady-state conditions. Longitudinal studies are warranted.

articles.title: Elevated pleural pressure, airway closure, and the physiological difference between positive- and negative-pressure ventilation.
articles.authors: Jan van Egmond, Jan Paul Mulier, Tom Schepens

articles.title: Neural correlates underlying motor sequence task performance: handedness and sequence complexity.
articles.authors: János Négyesi, Jun Zhao, Yifan Wang et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: We aimed to determine the neural correlates of motor sequence performance in healthy young adults, with respect to handedness and sequence complexity. METHODS: Strongly left-handed (LH, n = 15, 24.9y) and right-handed (RH, n = 15, 26.4y) participants performed finger key presses on a numeric keypad at four levels of sequence complexity with each hand in a randomized order. RESULTS: Both LH and RH performed the motor sequence task with faster reaction and motor execution times when using their right hand, irrespective of sequence complexity. Increasing motor-sequence complexity reduced frontal and parietal EEG power in both LH and RH, particularly at the highest complexity level, while RH also showed increased occipital delta activity when using the non-dominant hand, indicating that both sequence complexity and handedness modulate cortical activity during motor sequence performance. In addition, connectivity analysis showed significant hemispheric differences in brain network organization across frequency bands, with mainly greater left-hemisphere frontal and occipital connectivity but stronger right-hemisphere parietal connectivity. Sequence complexity primarily influenced functional connectivity (wPLI) rather than network topology. Notably, connectivity measures and selected MST-derived graph-theoretical metrics were linked to motor performance. CONCLUSION: Our findings suggest that motor-sequence performance is faster with the right hand, regardless of handedness and sequence complexity, which relies on a consistently organized hemispheric network, while increasing task complexity is managed primarily through frequency-specific changes in functional connectivity rather than large-scale reorganization of network structure.

articles.title: Semilunar nucleus neurons are highly excitable and potentiated by group I mGluRs to drive descending excitation to the mouse MNTB.
articles.authors: Huimei Wang, Xiaoyu Wang, Danah Alquraish et al.
articles.abstract: Medial nucleus of the trapezoid body (MNTB) neurons receive one of the largest synapses in the mammalian brain, the calyx of Held; however, multiple studies reported additional non-calyceal excitatory inputs of largely unresolved origin to MNTB neurons. Most recently, the semilunar nucleus (SLN) was identified as a potential source of such non-calyceal input in the rat. To elucidate the function of this novel pathway, we investigated the connectivity and physiology of the mouse SLN, with particular focus on neuromodulation by group I metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluRs). Viral tracing not only confirmed the SLN-MNTB pathway in mice, but also revealed that MNTB-projecting SLN neurons received their input from the ipsilateral auditory cortex. Physiological characterization of SLN neurons using whole-cell patch-clamp recordings showed that SLN neurons, unlike most other auditory brainstem neurons, were intrinsically highly excitable. Electrical stimulation of the fibre tracts located dorsal to the SLN, evoked small, slow AMPA receptor-mediated EPSCs in SLN neurons that readily summated temporally. Immunolabeling revealed a heterogeneous expression of mGluR1 and mGluR5 across SLN neurons. A subpopulation of SLN neurons exhibited spontaneous action potential firing at resting membrane potential. Pharmacological activation of group I mGluRs further increased spontaneous firing of SLN neurons. Probing for functional connectivity between SLN and the ipsilateral MNTB, fibre tracts dorsal and lateral to the MNTB were stimulated, eliciting primarily non-calyceal AMPA receptor-mediated EPSCs in MNTB neurons. These findings suggest that SLN output may provide a glutamatergic tonic drive to MNTB neurons, potentially modulating their temporal processing. KEY POINTS: MNTB receives a descending input from the ipsilateral auditory cortex via SLN. SLN neurons are highly excitable during development and into maturation, with a subset exhibiting spontaneous firing at resting membrane potential. Descending glutamatergic input to SLN is small and slow, and shows consistent temporal summation. Group I mGluRs further enhance spontaneous firing of SLN neurons and both mGluR1 and mGluR5 are expressed in the SLN. Descending ipsilateral projections to MNTB neurons primarily drive glutamatergic, non-calyceal inputs.

articles.title: Six Weeks of Drop Jump Training on Stable Versus Unstable Landing Surfaces Result in Similar Improvements in Drop Jumping Performance in Young Healthy Men.
articles.journal: Journal of strength and conditioning research
articles.authors: Lysander Pollitt, Olaf Prieske, David G Behm et al.
articles.abstract: Pollitt, L, Pieske, O, Behm, DG, and Granacher, U. Six weeks of drop jump training on stable vs. unstable landing surfaces result in similar improvements in drop jumping performance in young healthy men. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-To investigate how progressive drop jump (DJ) training performed on unstable landing surfaces affects jumping performance. Forty-two subjects were randomly allocated to no training (CONTROL, n = 8), stable surface (STABLE, n = 9), or 1 of 3 unstable landing conditions: mini-trampoline (n = 9), both-sides-used balance trainer (BOSU, n = 8), or an equated volume of BOSU and STABLE (MIX, n = 8). Subjects in each experimental condition completed 1,080 jumps across 9 drop heights (0.2 m progressing to 1 m) during 3 sessions per week over 6 weeks. Pre- and post-testing assessed maximal DJ at low (0.2 m), moderate (0.6 m), and high (1 m) drop heights for reactive strength index (RSI), jump height (JH), and contact time (CT). Using baseline as a covariate, analysis of covariance revealed significant, large main effects of condition for DJ outcome measures across all drop heights (0.19 < ηp2< 0.48). Bonferroni-adjusted post hoc comparisons identified significant postintervention differences between certain experimental conditions and CONTROL, depending on the outcome measure. No significant differences were observed between experimental conditions. At 0.2 m, differences in CT (p = 0.016) and RSI (p = 0.003) were observed for BOSU. At 0.6 m, CT for BOSU (p = 0.033), JH for STABLE (p = 0.034), and RSI for STABLE (p = 0.012) and BOSU (p = 0.013). At 1 m, JH for MIX (p = 0.012), and RSI (p ≤ 0.003) for all experimental conditions. Progressive DJ training on unstable training devices resulted in changes in performance comparable to a stable landing surface. When conceptualizing training programs, including plyometrics performed on unstable landing surfaces may provide an alternative neuromuscular stimulus without compromising performance.

articles.title: Adaptive Responses to "Top-up" Repeated-Sprint Training in Hypoxia or Normoxia in Male University Basketball Players.
articles.journal: International journal of sports physiology and performance
articles.authors: Masahiro Hagiwara, Takaki Yamagishi, Daichi Yamashita
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Repeated-sprint training in hypoxia (RSH) has been shown to provide greater performance benefits than similar training in normoxia (RSN), whereas little is known regarding beneficial effects of RSH following a block of RSN. This study aimed to determine adaptive responses to "top-up" RSH. METHODS: After pretesting, 15 male university basketball players completed 6 RSN sessions (2 sets of five to seven 6-second cycle sprints, 30-second intersprint, and 5-min interset recovery), followed by midtesting. Participants were then allocated to either hypoxic (HYP, n = 8) or normoxic (NOR, n = 7) group and completed 6 "top-up" sessions (3 sets of identical protocol), with 5 RSH (3000 m) plus 1 RSN in HYP and 6 RSN in NOR. Six-second and incremental cycle tests were performed to determine 1-second peak power (PP6s), 6-second mean power (MP6s), maximal aerobic power (MAP), and peak oxygen uptake (V˙O2peak) at pre, mid, and post. Repeated-sprint ability (PPRSA; averaged peak power over 10 sprints) was assessed during sessions 2, 6, and 12 in normoxia. RESULTS: A 2-way mixed analysis of variance revealed main effects of time (P < .05, partial η2 = .349-.537) in all test variables (PP6s: Δ 10.6% [13.8%], MP6s: Δ 12.2% [13.6%], MAP: Δ 5.3% [4.3%], V˙O2peak: Δ 6.1% [5.5%]) without time-by-group interaction, whereas neither group improved PPRSA. CONCLUSIONS: Twelve sessions of repeated-sprint training improved anaerobic and aerobic capacities in male basketball players, with no additional benefit of hypoxic exposure during the second training phase, suggesting increased training volume may have outweighed the environmental factor.

articles.title: Case Study Insights Into Female World-Class and Elite Athletes' Training and Physiology.
articles.journal: International journal of sports physiology and performance
articles.authors: Guro Strøm Solli, Tilda Harju, Daichi Yamashita et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: This article offers a structured overview of published case studies involving elite and world-class female Olympic athletes, highlighting the unique insights these studies provide into training characteristics, physiology, performance, and female-specific factors. METHODS: Four databases were systematically searched for peer-reviewed case studies involving tiers 4 to 5 female Olympic athletes reporting individual-level data on training, physiological, and/or performance characteristics. RESULTS: Thirty-eight studies describing 54 elite and world-class female athletes from 18 countries and 19 Olympic sports met the inclusion criteria. Most studies were published after 2017 (68%), originated from Europe (58%), and involved endurance sports (81%). Fifteen studies examined long-term athlete development, with observation periods ranging from 4 to 26 years. Fourteen studies reported annual training and physiological characteristics across 10 sports including training volume, intensity distribution, periodization, and physiological profiling. Four studies examined altitude training, 8 addressed competition demands, tapering, and precompetition strategies, and 8 focused on female-specific physiology, health, and performance, including energy availability, menstrual function, hormonal cycle monitoring and pregnancy, and postpartum return to sport. CONCLUSION: Case studies provide unique athlete-centered insights into the complex interactions between training, physiology, health, and performance in elite female athletes. Collectively, they demonstrate that pathways to world-class performance are highly individualized, while generating hypotheses that complement group-based research. Future case studies should prioritize underrepresented sports, geographical regions, and female-specific topics to expand the diversity of performance environments and athlete populations represented in the literature.

articles.title: Lumping vs. Splitting Nutrients, Foods and Diet Patterns in Nutrition Research: Science Dialogue Mapping of Origins, Uses and Knowledge Gaps.
articles.authors: Sabrina Ayoub-Charette, Laura Chiavaroli, Alexandra E Cowan-Pyle et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: The practices of lumping together and splitting apart foods, nutrients, and diet patterns shape the interpretation of nutritional evidence and guidance. OBJECTIVE & METHODS: To discuss the inherent complexity of 'lumping' and 'splitting' foods, nutrients, and diet patterns, we held an in-person colloquium in December 2024, where we utilized dialogue mapping to summarize the discussion in real-time. Knowledgeable early-career nutrition researchers explored the contexts for lumping and splitting with the goal of beginning a conversation in the scientific community on the topic. RESULTS: Six themes emerged about lumping or splitting: definitions and history, population heterogeneity, consumer behavior, policy and public health messaging, frameworks for categorization, and measurement and methods. Participants identified lumping that persists on historical rather than scientific grounds, with circularity in policy in which guidelines are used to build adherence indices that are then used to evaluate those guidelines. The shifting protein categories across successive Dietary Guidelines for Americans Scientific Reports showed the same foods being lumped or split for different purposes. Measurement error and incomplete food composition data limit splitting, whereas life stage, physiology, and culture favored finer categories. CONCLUSIONS: Participants emphasized that lumping and splitting are not inherently right or wrong, nor are they inherently a binary approach; rather, the appropriateness to lump or split depends on the purpose of the analysis, public health messaging, or evidence-informed policy decisions. Future work is needed to operationalize lumping and splitting decisions in the field of nutrition science, and to enhance transparency in the rationale of lumping and splitting decisions.

articles.title: A vegetarian meal reduces protein digestibility without altering postprandial protein utilization in old rats.
articles.authors: M Muziot, M Andriamihaja, M Dufay et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: The composition of the meal, particularly its plants-based components, may reduce protein digestibility and amino acid (AA) availability. This issue is particularly relevant given the increasing adoption of plant-based diets, especially in populations with higher protein requirements, including older adults. OBJECTIVE: To assess the acute effects of meal context on pea protein and AA digestibility and metabolism across lifespan, comparing vegetarian and omnivorous meals. METHODS: 48 male Wistar rats aged 1, 10, and 18 months (n=16/age) consumed 15N-labeled peas within an omnivorous or vegetarian meal and were euthanized 6 h later. Digestive contents were collected for protein and AA digestibility. Plasma and urinary 15N enrichment was measured to evaluate deamination. Liver and muscle protein synthesis was determined using 13C-valine flooding dose method. Gene expression related to digestion and protein metabolism was quantified in liver, muscle, and intestinal mucosa. RESULTS: Fecal pea protein and caecal AA digestibility were slightly reduced with the vegetarian meal (93.5% vs. 94.7%, P = 0.01 and 90.5% vs. 93.7%, P = 0.0009, respectively), particularly in old rats (92.5% vs. 94.2%, P = 0.03 and 89.7% vs. 93.6%, P = 0.02, respectively). However, this reduction did not affect nitrogen utilization or protein synthesis. Young rats showed greater peripheral nitrogen utilization, with higher muscle protein synthesis (+70%, P < 0.0001) and lower deamination (-70%, P < 0.0001), consistent with growth demands. Adult and old rats exhibited higher liver protein synthesis (+40%, P = 0.0004) and higher deamination (+70%, P < 0.0001), indicating a shift toward maintenance metabolism, independent of meal type. CONCLUSIONS: The vegetarian meal slightly reduced protein and AA digestibility, likely due to its higher antinutritional factor content, with greater sensitivity in older rats, but did not impair postprandial protein metabolism. Long-term studies should determine whether these reductions have cumulative effects on muscle maintenance during aging. STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE: This study provides novel evidence that the negative impact of complex vegetarian meals on protein digestibility may be amplified with aging, while postprandial protein utilization remains preserved despite reduced digestibility. It further demonstrates that age-related shifts toward increased splanchnic retention and amino acid oxidation predominate over meal composition effects, highlighting aging as a key determinant of plant protein utilization.

articles.title: Lifestyle counseling including the DASH diet improves multiple metabolomic profiles.
articles.authors: Mahya Mehri Hajmir, Xichen Wang, Rob M van Dam
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Lifestyle interventions improve cardiometabolic risk factors, but data from randomized trials on their impact on detailed metabolomic profiles remain limited. OBJECTIVES: Our aim was to evaluate the effects of lifestyle counseling with and without the Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DASH) diet on changes in metabolomic patterns. METHODS: We analyzed data from 690 adult participants of the randomized PREMIER trial. The trial compared three lifestyle interventions: 'Advice-only', 'Established', and 'Established plus DASH'. Fasting plasma metabolites were quantified by NMR spectroscopy at baseline and 6 months, and principal component (PC) analysis was used to identify metabolomic patterns. Multiple linear regression examined the interventions and changes in BMI and heart rate in relation to changes in PC scores and individual metabolites. RESULTS: Thirteen PCs representing lipoprotein, triglyceride-rich, amino acid, fatty acid, inflammatory, and ketone-related patterns were identified. Compared with Advice-only, the Established intervention reduced PC4 (β = -0.50, P = 0.04), VLDL cholesterol, and saturated fatty acids. Established plus DASH had broader effects, reducing PC9 (β = -0.33, P = 0.01), PC11 (β = -0.28 P = 0.004), and PC12 (β = -0.23, P = 0.02), increasing omega-3 fatty acids, and lowering branched-chain and aromatic amino acids, lactate, citrate, and GlycA. BMI change was associated with multiple PCs, whereas heart rate change showed fewer independent associations. CONCLUSIONS: Lifestyle interventions induce coordinated metabolomic changes across lipid, amino acid, and inflammatory pathways. Weight loss appears to be the primary driver, while adding DASH provides broader metabolomic benefits than standard lifestyle counseling. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00000616 (PREMIER: Lifestyle Interventions for Blood Pressure Control - Full Text View - ClinicalTrials.gov).

articles.title: Children at risk of vitamin A deficiency exhibit taxonomic dysbiosis and functional remodeling of the gut microbiome: a matched case-control study.
articles.authors: Sofia Moran-Ramos, Johan Alvarado-Calderon, Daniel Cerqueda-Garcia et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Vitamin A deficiency is one of the most prevalent micronutrient deficiencies worldwide. This condition increases susceptibility to infections and due to its role in intestinal barrier integrity, it has been suggested that it could predispose to gut dysbiosis. OBJECTIVE: The aim of the study was to identify whether the gut microbiome of school-aged children at risk of vitamin A deficiency is associated with a dysbiotic state. METHODS: This 1:2 matched case-control study for children at risk of vitamin A deficiency included thirteen school-aged children (6-9 years old) at risk of VAD and 26 with adequate vitamin A levels (VAA) from the ORSMEC cohort. Habitual diet was determined with a FFQ, plasma retinol levels were determined through HPLC, and gut microbial characterization was performed through shotgun sequencing. RESULTS: In the present study, children at risk of VAD showed significantly higher levels of serum CRP (P=0.026). Although taxonomic gut microbial characterization showed no differences in alpha or beta diversity among groups, children at risk of VAD showed an enrichment of some facultative anaerobes, proposed to be established pathogens mainly from Streptococcus and Enterococcus genera (PFDR<0.1). At a functional level vitamin A status explained 7.09% of the variation in gut microbial functionality, when evaluated with the Bray-Curtis dissimilarity metric (P=0.008). Specifically, pathways related to pathogenicity such as O-antigen biosynthesis, heme biosynthesis and ethanolamine utilization were significantly enriched in children at risk of VAD (PFDR<0.1). In contrast, abundance of pathways related to B vitamins metabolism such as folate transformations, the super pathway for Coenzyme A biosynthesis and its precursor phosphopantothenate (vitamin B5) were depleted (PFDR<0.1). CONCLUSION: Overall, our study showed that in school-aged children, being at risk of vitamin A deficiency is associated with an enrichment of potential pathobionts and a shift in gut microbial functionality that could be related to greater pathogenicity.

articles.title: Metabolism Meets Epigenetics: β-Hydroxybutyrate-Driven Lysine β-Hydroxybutyrylation Bridging Energy Metabolism With Transcription and Protein Functional Remodeling.
articles.authors: Shaoqi Cheng, Chao Cheng, Jiaxin Zhou et al.
articles.abstract: β-Hydroxybutyrate (BHB) is the primary product of ketone body metabolism. Beyond serving as an energy source, BHB plays a crucial role in metabolic regulation, anti-inflammatory and antioxidative responses, immune modulation, and neuroprotection. Circulating BHB levels are closely linked to dietary composition and lifestyle. Medium-chain fatty acids, fasting, ketogenic diets, and moderate exercise promote BHB production, and exogenous ketone supplements can rapidly elevate BHB without the need for carbohydrate restriction. Studies have shown that BHB can regulate gene expression through epigenetic modifications, with lysine β-hydroxybutyrylation (Kbhb) establishing a crucial link between ketone body metabolism and gene regulation. Kbhb modulates chromatin accessibility, gene transcription, and cellular metabolism, and its substrates extend beyond histones to include non-histone proteins. Consequently, this modification is essential for maintaining physiological homeostasis and regulating disease processes. Despite substantial progress in Kbhb research, its precise regulatory mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Histone deacetylases (HDACs) and the sirtuin (SIRT) family function as "erasers" (enzymes that catalyze the removal of specific post-translational modifications from histone and non-histone proteins), whereas E1A-binding protein p300 and its homolog CREB-binding protein (p300/CBP) act as "writers" (enzymes that catalyze the addition of specific post-translational modifications to histone and non-histone proteins), both playing pivotal roles in the dynamic regulation of Kbhb modification. This review summarizes the biological functions of BHB and Kbhb, emphasizing their roles in metabolic regulation, their nutritional connections, epigenetic modifications, and disease development.
